title: Percentiles: definition, method and practice
summary: Sort, compute the index i = (p/100) x n, then round up or average two values. Worked: 80th percentile of 70 values, the 20 richest individuals, and the 15 retail stores.

chunks.heading: What a percentile is
chunks.explanation_md:
A **percentile** tells you **how the data are spread over the interval from the smallest value to the largest value**.

The **pth percentile** is a value such that **at least p per cent of the items take on this value or less**, and **at least (100 - p) per cent of the items take on this value or more**.

Example of reading it: if a value is the 80th percentile, at least 80% of items are at or below it and at least 20% are at or above it.

key_terms.meaning: The pth percentile is a value such that at least p per cent of the items are at or below it and at least (100 - p) per cent are at or above it.

chunks.heading: The computation method
chunks.explanation_md:
**Steps:**
1. **Arrange the data in ascending order.**
2. **Compute the index** i = (p/100) × n, the position of the pth percentile.
3. If **i is not an integer, round up**; the pth percentile is the value in that position.
4. If **i is an integer**, the pth percentile is the **average of the values in the ith and (i + 1)th positions**.

**Slide example (70 values):** i = (80/100) × 70 = **56** (an integer), so average the 56th and 57th values: **80th percentile = (535 + 549)/2 = 542**.

Reading it: 56/70 = 0.8 or 80%, so **at least 80% of items are 542 or less**; 14/70 = 0.2 or 20%, so **at least 20% are 542 or more**.
chunks.exam_line: i = (p/100)n. Not an integer: round up. Integer: average of the ith and (i+1)th values. Example: i = 56, (535 + 549)/2 = 542.

chunks.heading: Practice: the 20 richest individuals
chunks.explanation_md:
**Data (2007 net worth, billions of dollars, 20 values):** sorted ascending: 18, 18, 18, 18, 19, 20, 20, 20, 21, 22, 22, 23, 24, 26, 27, 32, 33, 49, 52, 56.

**50th percentile:** i = (50/100) × 20 = 10 (integer). Average the 10th and 11th values: (22 + 22)/2 = **22**.

**80th percentile:** i = (80/100) × 20 = 16 (integer). Average the 16th and 17th values: (32 + 33)/2 = **32.5**.

The 50th percentile is the median, 22, which matches the median marked on the dot plot with the mode at 18 and the mean at 26.9.

chunks.heading: Practice: the retail chain with 15 stores
chunks.explanation_md:
**Data (monthly sales, ₹ lakhs):** 28, 34, 31, 41, 38, 27, 32, 36, 34, 30, 29, 44, 35, 39, 30 (stores 1 to 15). Sorted: 27, 28, 29, 30, 30, 31, 32, 34, 34, 35, 36, 38, 39, 41, 44.

**1. Stores below the average:** mean = 508 / 15 = 33.87. Stores below it: store 1 (28), 3 (31), 6 (27), 7 (32), 10 (30), 11 (29), 15 (30). These may need support or a revised strategy.

**2. Cluster:** two values repeat: 34 (stores 2 and 9) and 30 (stores 10 and 15). Those are the modes, so the data is bimodal. Investigate the common feature of those stores (location, management style, product mix).

**3. Four equal groups (quartiles):** n = 15. Q1: i = 3.75, round up to the 4th value = **30**. Q2: i = 7.5, round up to the 8th value = **34**. Q3: i = 11.25, round up to the 12th value = **38**. Stores at or below 30 form the lowest group (urgent intervention or training); stores above 38 form the top group (study for best practice).

**4. Top 10%:** 90th percentile: i = 13.5, round up to the 14th value = **41**. Stores at or above 41 (store 4 at 41 and store 12 at 44) get the special rewards.
chunks.exam_line: 15 stores: mean 33.87; Q1 30, median 34, Q3 38; 90th percentile 41 (stores 4 and 12).

questions.stem: Explain how to calculate a percentile and interpret it. Illustrate with the 80th percentile of the 70-value data set.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Introduction.** A percentile shows how the data is spread from the smallest to the largest value.

**Definition.** The pth percentile is a value such that at least p per cent of items take this value or less and at least (100 - p) per cent take this value or more. Quartiles are specific percentiles: Q1 = 25th, Q2 = 50th (median), Q3 = 75th.

**Method.** Arrange in ascending order; i = (p/100) × n; if i is not an integer round up and take that position; if it is an integer average the ith and (i + 1)th values.

**Example.** n = 70, p = 80: i = (80/100) × 70 = 56, an integer, so average the 56th and 57th values: (535 + 549)/2 = **542**.

**Interpretation.** 56/70 = 0.8: at least 80% of items are 542 or less. 14/70 = 0.2: at least 20% are 542 or more.

**Conclusion.** The same steps give any percentile.

rubric.point: Method steps and the two rules

questions.stem: A retail chain has 15 stores with monthly sales (₹ lakhs) 28, 34, 31, 41, 38, 27, 32, 36, 34, 30, 29, 44, 35, 39, 30. Identify the below-average stores, any cluster, the quartiles and the stores for the top 10% reward.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Sorted data:** 27, 28, 29, 30, 30, 31, 32, 34, 34, 35, 36, 38, 39, 41, 44 (n = 15).

**1. Below average.** Mean = 508/15 = 33.87. Stores below it: store 1 (28), 3 (31), 6 (27), 7 (32), 10 (30), 11 (29) and 15 (30). They may need support or a revised strategy.

**2. Cluster.** The values 34 (stores 2 and 9) and 30 (stores 10 and 15) repeat, so the data is bimodal. Investigate what these stores share (location, management style, product mix).

**3. Quartiles.** Q1: i = 3.75, round up to the 4th value = 30. Q2: i = 7.5, 8th value = 34. Q3: i = 11.25, 12th value = 38. Stores at or below 30 form the lowest group (urgent intervention or training); stores above 38 are the top group to study for best practice.

**4. Top 10%.** 90th percentile: i = 13.5, round up to the 14th value = 41. Stores at or above 41 (store 4 and store 12) earn the incentive.

**Conclusion.** The percentile method gives clear cut-offs for support and reward.
